tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=offsets < n_elements)
tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y)
None of them; tl.store never writes out of bounds
explain: Without a mask the last program writes all BLOCK_SIZE lanes, including addresses past the end of the output buffer. That corrupts neighboring memory or faults. The first two are the same mask written two ways.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
question: A tokenizer downsamples by 16 in each direction. How many image positions does a 512 x 512 image take, not counting BOI and EOI?
explain: 512 / 16 = 32 per side, and 32 x 32 = 1024. This matches Chameleon, whose tokenizer turns a 512 x 512 image into 1024 tokens. 32 is only one side; 4096 is what an f = 8 tokenizer gives.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: One encoder or two: why Janus splits seeing from drawing
question: In the Janus ablation, replacing the shared VQ tokenizer with decoupled SigLIP + VQ raised MMBench from 35.0 to 69.4 while FID moved from 8.72 to 8.53. What does that suggest?
options: Generation quality was the bottleneck
The transformer was too small
A reconstruction-oriented tokenizer gives poor semantic features for understanding, and a dedicated understanding encoder fixes that without hurting generation
MMBench rewards image resolution only
explain: Generation was about the same in both rows, so the gain is almost all understanding. VQ codes are trained to rebuild pixels, not to expose meaning; SigLIP is trained to align images with text.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Concurrency in one address space: cooperative threads and no fork
question: A service forks a worker process per connection. A team wants to run it on Unikraft with the multiprocess option of posix-process enabled. What should they expect?
options: fork works, since the multiprocess level emulates it with copy-on-write pages
fork works, but each child gets its own VM
The service runs unchanged if it is built as PIE
There is no copying fork; they need a thread-based mode or a redesign, since vfork only borrows the parent's memory until execve or exit
explain: One address space cannot hold a second copy at the same addresses. posix-process offers vfork plus execve (of PIE programs) at its multiprocess level, which suits launching another program, not cloning a worker. Many servers can run as one process instead: the Unikraft catalog runs nginx with `master_process off` and one worker.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Hands-on: build, boot and measure a unikernel
question: You time `kraft run unikraft.org/nginx:1.25` for the first time on a fresh machine and it takes several seconds. Before blaming the VMM, what should you rule out?
options: That nginx is compiled with a slow allocator
That the VM has too much memory
That lwip needs seconds to negotiate DHCP on every boot
That kraft spent the time downloading the OCI image (the standard container image format kraft packages unikernels in), which it does on first use; time a second run
explain: The kraft docs say an OCI image not present on the host is downloaded before it is executed. A fair boot measurement excludes that, and separates the VMM's share from the guest's.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum
question: hnswlib builds an inner-product index with d = 100. Which kernel does it pick on an AVX machine?
options: The SIMD16 kernel with a 4-element scalar tail
The pure scalar loop
The SIMD4 kernel, since 100 is a multiple of 4
The AVX-512 kernel with a masked tail
explain: The dispatch checks d % 16 first, then d % 4. 100 is not a multiple of 16 but is a multiple of 4, so the SIMD4 kernel covers all 100 elements with no tail. The residual kernels are used only when neither divides d.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch
question: Two roles are mapped to the same ResourcePool and fused with create_colocated_worker_cls. What is the main effect?
options: Both roles run in one Ray actor per GPU and share one CUDA and distributed context
Both roles get disjoint halves of the pool's GPUs
The roles run concurrently on the GPU with separate memory pools
The roles are forced to use the same model weights
explain: Same pool means same GPUs; fusing the classes avoids one process per role per GPU. The roles still run one after another in the order the controller calls them. Disjoint GPUs require different pools.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and tuning verl in practice
question: Same Qwen3-8B setup: 12.29 GB of training state stays on each GPU. Which change lets you run vLLM at gpu_memory_utilization 0.85 without exceeding 80 GB in this simplified budget?
options: Enable actor param_offload and optimizer_offload, which move the training state to CPU between updates
Raise ppo_max_token_len_per_gpu
Set rollout.free_cache_engine=False
Lower data.train_batch_size
explain: At 0.85 vLLM alone takes 68 GB, and 68 + 12.29 = 80.3 GB. Offloading parameters and optimizer state frees that 12.29 GB during rollout at the cost of copy time each step. The token budget affects only the trainer's micro-batches, keeping the KV cache makes things worse, and the batch size does not change either allocation.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Algorithms as config: critics, estimators and rollout correction
question: A run sets algorithm.rollout_correction.bypass_mode=true with loss_type=ppo_clip. What changes per step?
options: The old_log_prob stage is skipped: the rollout's log-probs become pi_old, and the PPO ratio pi_theta / pi_rollout handles the correction
Rollout log-probs are no longer needed
IS weights are now applied twice
The reference model is skipped
explain: Bypass mode sets pi_old equal to pi_rollout, so the trainer copies rollout_log_probs into old_log_probs instead of running compute_log_prob, saving a forward pass (and, in separate_async, the pi_old CPU transfers). It still needs the engine's log-probs; the reference model is unrelated.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
question: Why do MovieChat and MA-LMM only merge temporally adjacent frames instead of the globally most similar pair?
options: Global similarity is impossible to compute
Adjacent merging keeps temporal order, so each merged token still stands for one contiguous stretch of time
Adjacent frames are always identical
It makes the LLM context longer
explain: If the speaker returns to the same slide at minute 5 and minute 50, a global merge would fuse two distant moments into one token and destroy the timeline. Adjacent merging keeps each memory slot contiguous and ordered.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Latent actions: a controller learned from unlabelled video
question: A model's $\Delta_t\mathrm{PSNR}$ is close to 0. What does that tell you?
options: The video quality is very high
The tokenizer failed to reconstruct frames
The model is perfectly controllable
Random actions produce frames about as close to the truth as inferred actions, so the actions barely control the output
explain: If swapping the true latent actions for random ones does not change how far the prediction lands from the real frame, the model is mostly ignoring the action input. High controllability shows up as a large positive gap.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: The hypervisor as a security boundary: who must not reach whom
question: A cloud provider worries about one customer's VM reading another customer's memory through shared CPU caches, with no software bug involved. Which attack direction is that?
options: Host-to-guest
Guest-to-guest
Guest-to-host
It is not a virtualization problem
explain: The attacker is a guest and the victim is another guest. The path runs through shared hardware rather than a hypervisor bug, which is why lesson 13 treats flushing and core isolation as hypervisor duties.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Device emulation: the attack surface the guest controls
question: The virtio spec forbids drivers from building descriptor loops. Why must the device still check for loops?
options: Because the driver may be malicious; an unchecked loop would make the device spin or walk memory forever
Because the spec also requires it of devices
Because loops are allowed in packed virtqueues
It need not; the IOMMU breaks loops
explain: A requirement on drivers constrains only honest drivers. The device runs on the host and processes hostile input, so it bounds chain length itself. The toy rejects a chain after QUEUE_SIZE descriptors.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: the 2025 ESXi escape chain, VMSA-2025-0004
question: In VMSA-2025-0004, why was CVE-2025-22225 (kernel write) needed if CVE-2025-22224 already gave code execution?
options: It was not needed; the two are alternatives
22225 was needed to log in to the guest first
22224 gives code execution only as the per-VM VMX process, which is sandboxed; 22225 lets code in that process write the kernel and escape the sandbox
22225 bypasses the IOMMU
explain: Broadcom's own text: 22224 yields execution 'as the virtual machine's VMX process', and 22225 lets an actor 'with privileges within the VMX process' trigger a kernel write 'leading to an escape of the sandbox'. The sandbox forced a chain.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Confidential VMs: SEV-SNP, TDX and Arm CCA stop trusting the host
question: In TDX and Arm CCA alike, guest memory is split into protected and shared parts. Which data should a well-built confidential guest put in shared memory?
options: Only data meant for the host, such as I/O buffers, ideally already encrypted by the guest
Kernel stacks and page tables
Disk encryption keys, so the host can back them up
Nothing; shared memory is unused
explain: Linux's TDX docs: 'Shared mappings must never be used for sensitive memory content'. Shared pages exist for I/O and communication with the host, which controls them completely.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
question: A colleague proposes ViT-B with 16 heads instead of 12 (D stays 768) to get more capacity. How does the parameter count of a block change?
options: It stays the same: each head gets 48 dims instead of 64
It grows by one third, since each head has its own Q, K, V
It doubles, because attention cost is quadratic
It shrinks, because the MLP gets smaller
explain: Multi-head attention splits the D = 768 output columns of Q, K and V among the heads. With 16 heads each head has 768 / 16 = 48 dims; the matrices are still 768 x 768. More heads changes how capacity is used, not how many weights exist.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
question: During a robot task, RT-2 restricts decoding to valid action tokens only. What failure does this prevent?
options: The model running out of GPU memory
Cross-entropy loss becoming negative
The model answering with ordinary words that cannot be turned into a robot command
Image tokens being emitted as output
explain: RT-2 must output something executable. Constraining the output vocabulary to the 256 action tokens on robot prompts guarantees a parsable action, while the same model still answers normal vision-language questions with full text.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
question: You must control a 14-dim bimanual robot at 50 Hz for laundry folding, where demonstrators fold in different orders. Which action head fits best?
options: Per-step 256-bin tokens, since it needs no extra modules
Mean-squared-error regression of one action per step
A flow-matching action expert that outputs 50-step chunks
Per-step tokens with a larger vocabulary
explain: Per-step tokens would need 700 tokens per second; regression averages different folding strategies. A flow-matching expert produces continuous 50-step chunks in one short loop and samples one mode, which is what pi0 was built for.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: VQGAN: perceptual and adversarial losses for 256-token images
question: A VQGAN's adversarial loss starts dominating training and reconstructions drift away from the input. Which part of the method is designed to prevent this?
options: The commitment loss weight beta
The straight-through estimator
The adaptive weight lambda, computed from gradient norms at the last decoder layer
The sliding attention window used at sampling time
explain: lambda = grad of L_rec / (grad of L_GAN + delta) at the last decoder layer. When the GAN gradient grows relative to the reconstruction gradient, lambda falls, scaling the adversarial term down.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
question: Which piece declares that a backend needs compute capability 8.0 or higher?
options: The `AttentionImpl` instance, by checking the GPU inside `forward`
The metadata builder, by raising during `build()`
The `AttentionBackend` class, through `supports_compute_capability`, which selection calls before anything runs
The scheduler, which skips requests on unsupported GPUs
explain: Capabilities live on the backend class so they can be checked at startup. `validate_configuration` calls `supports_compute_capability` along with the head size, dtype, KV dtype and block size checks.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
question: A ViT with 14 x 14 patches runs on a 448 x 448 input with no pooling. How many patch tokens does it produce?
explain: $448 / 14 = 32$ patches per side, and $32 \cdot 32 = 1024$. 32 is only the side length, and 576 is the count for 336 x 336 input. Token count grows with the square of the side length.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Reading a receipt into validated JSON
question: Which extraction error would the two arithmetic checks in this lesson NOT catch?
options: A unit price misread from 8.75 as 3.75
The merchant name misread as a similar name
A subtotal misread from 21.55 as 27.55
A total misread from 23.27 as 28.27
explain: Price, subtotal and total errors all break one of the sums. The merchant name takes part in no arithmetic, so it needs another check, such as matching against a known merchant list, or human review.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: A practical wait-free queue: phases and helping (Kogan-Petrank)
question: A thread on an otherwise idle 64-thread system calls `enq()` on the base Kogan-Petrank queue. Roughly how much work does it do?
options: Constant work, like the Michael-Scott queue
Work proportional to 64, because maxPhase() and help() each scan the whole state array
Unbounded work, since helping can repeat forever
Work proportional to the queue length
explain: Even with no contention the base version reads every descriptor twice: once to compute the phase and once in help(). The paper's optimizations replace maxPhase() with an atomic counter and make help() check one or a few entries per call in cyclic order, which keeps the bound but cuts the uncontended cost.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Inside the models: a multimesh GNN and a 3D Earth transformer
question: Why does GraphCast run its 16 processor layers on a multimesh instead of directly on the 721 x 1440 grid with nearest-neighbor edges?
options: Because GNNs cannot represent grids
Because the multimesh has more nodes than the grid, giving higher resolution
With only local edges, 16 layers move information only about 16 cells, and the lat-lon grid is very uneven near the poles
Because the multimesh lets the model skip the decoder
explain: Each message-passing layer moves information one edge. Long coarse-level edges let a few layers reach across the globe, and the icosahedral mesh is near-uniform. The mesh has fewer nodes (40,962) than the grid (about 1 million).

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Web testing as work: pentests, disclosure programmes and bounties
question: Two researchers report different requests that exploit the same missing check, fixed by one code change. Under GitLab's duplicate rule, what happens?
options: Both are paid in full
The first validated report for that fix is rewarded; the other is a duplicate
The second is paid half
Neither is paid because the bug was found twice
explain: GitLab says it may reward the first report validated for a fix and treat later reports addressed by the same mitigation as duplicates, regardless of the attack vector. Bounties pay for root causes, not for variations.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Recon at bounty scale: wildcards, subdomains and live hosts
question: Why does the scope filter check exclusions before the wildcard?
options: Exclusions are shorter strings
Because an excluded host also matches the wildcard, and exclusion must win
fnmatch cannot match wildcards otherwise
To make the scan faster
explain: Excluded hosts usually sit inside the wildcard (a vendor-run status page under the same domain). Checking the wildcard first would mark them in scope. Most specific rule, the exclusion, must win.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authorization at scale: two accounts and a replay matrix
question: In the toy app, why did GET /docs/1001 pass the replay while DELETE /docs/1001 failed?
options: DELETE requests are not logged
The ownership check was written only inside the GET branch
ben is an admin
404 and 200 mean the same thing
explain: The check `DOCS[doc] != user` ran only when method was GET. Other methods fell through to `return 200`. Method-specific checks are a classic source of partial authorization.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Reading a programme policy: scope, rules and safe harbour
question: Which of these would most likely void the protection of a disclose.io-style safe harbour?
options: Reporting a bug within a day of finding it
Telling the company you will publish the data you downloaded unless they pay
Using two test accounts you created
Asking the programme whether an asset is in scope
explain: The template's expectations include 'do not engage in extortion' and minimal data access. Demanding payment under threat is outside good faith and outside the policy.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: How a page loads: HTML, subresources, JavaScript and the DOM
question: Why can a script loaded from a third-party CDN (content delivery network, a company that serves files for other sites) read the cookies of the page that includes it (unless they are marked HttpOnly, a flag that hides them from scripts)?
options: Because CDNs are trusted by browsers by default
Because the CDN also sets the cookies
It cannot; scripts can only read cookies of the server they came from
Because an included script runs in the including page's context, with that page's origin
explain: The browser judges a script by the page it runs in, not by where its bytes came from. An included script is part of the page, so it gets the page's DOM, its non-HttpOnly cookies via document.cookie, and the ability to send requests as the page.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefixes
question: A session cookie is set with `SameSite=Lax; Secure; HttpOnly`. An attacker's page auto-submits a hidden form that POSTs to your /transfer endpoint. Does the cookie go with it?
options: Yes, because form submissions are top-level navigations
Yes, because HttpOnly cookies are always sent
No: Lax only sends on cross-site top-level navigations with a safe method, and POST is not safe
No, because Secure blocks all cross-site requests
explain: Lax requires both a top-level navigation and a safe method like GET. A cross-site POST fails the second test, so an explicitly Lax cookie is left off. (Chrome's default-Lax for cookies without the attribute has a two-minute exception, another reason to set it explicitly.)

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Frames and clickjacking: X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors
question: A page sends only `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`. Can an attacker's site frame it?
options: Only if the attacker's site is same-site
No, 'none' blocks everything including framing
No, because browsers block framing by default
Yes, because frame-ancestors does not fall back to default-src
explain: frame-ancestors is a navigation directive with no default-src fallback. Without frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options, any site may embed the page, which is also the browser default.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Site isolation: separate processes as a second wall
question: Why does Chrome's Site Isolation put processes per site rather than per origin?
options: Origins are too hard to compute
Because cookies are scoped per site
To stay compatible with pages that use document.domain to communicate across subdomains of one site
Per-origin processes are impossible on Windows
explain: Chromium's documentation says it uses sites instead of origins to avoid breaking existing pages that change document.domain to talk across subdomains. The cost is that same-site subdomains may share a process.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: PowerShell: objects in a pipeline, and why attackers like it
question: An attacker runs an obfuscated PowerShell command that decodes itself in memory and never touches disk. Which defender data source is most likely to show the actual code that ran?
options: The PowerShell execution policy setting
The list of installed programs
The NTFS permissions on powershell.exe
Script block logging (event 4104)
explain: Script block logging records the code PowerShell actually processes, after decoding. The execution policy is not a security boundary and records nothing.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: NTFS permissions and inheritance: reading and fixing an ACL
question: Why does a writable folder for a SYSTEM service turn any user into SYSTEM?
options: SYSTEM reads the user's token when it starts
Writable folders automatically grant SeDebugPrivilege
NTFS treats write as full control
The user can replace the program the service runs, and the service runs whatever is in that file with its own SYSTEM token
explain: The service's token is SYSTEM no matter who wrote the file. Control the file and you control what code runs with that token.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Event logs: anatomy of a record, and reading logons (4624, 4625)
question: Ana's account shows a 4624 with Logon Type 3 on a server Ana never uses, from Ana's workstation's IP address at 03:00. Why might this matter even though Ana's password was not typed?
options: Type 3 logons are always harmless
Type 3 means Ana was at the server's keyboard
Type 3 is only used by printers
A network logon can be made with stolen credential material such as an NTLM hash, so it fits credential theft on Ana's workstation
explain: Type 3 is a network logon. Pass the hash and remote admin tools produce exactly this, so an unusual type 3 at an odd hour is worth investigating alongside events on the source workstation.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Remote Desktop and BlueKeep: logons before login
question: A Windows Server 2008 R2 machine cannot be patched this week. Which single setting does CISA say effectively mitigates BlueKeep, and why?
options: Renaming port 3389
Turning on script block logging
Adding users to Remote Desktop Users
Enabling Network Level Authentication, because exploitation needs an unauthenticated session
explain: With NLA the session is only set up after authentication, and BlueKeep must be triggered in an unauthenticated session. Patching is still required, since an attacker with credentials is not stopped.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WEP: how a 24-bit IV broke Wi-Fi's first encryption
question: Two WEP frames are sent with the same IV and the same shared key. What does an eavesdropper gain by XORing the two ciphertexts?
options: The CRC-32 values of both frames, but nothing else
The shared WEP key directly
The XOR of the two plaintexts, because the identical keystreams cancel
Nothing, because the IV is encrypted
explain: Same IV plus same key means the same RC4 keystream. XORing the ciphertexts removes it and leaves p1 XOR p2; one guessed plaintext then reveals the other and the keystream itself.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA3: SAE, protected management frames and Enhanced Open
question: A network runs WPA3 transition mode (SAE and WPA2-PSK with the same password). What is the main residual risk Dragonblood identified?
options: Transition mode leaks the password in beacons
SAE can be decrypted passively
An attacker can lure WPA3-capable clients to a WPA2-only rogue network and record a handshake that allows offline guessing
PMF is disabled by WPA3
explain: Transition mode exists for backwards compatibility, and that compatibility is the attack: the WPA2 half reintroduces lesson 4's offline oracle. Moving to WPA3-only, or using transition_disable once all clients support SAE, closes it.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Public Wi-Fi and captive portals in the HTTPS era
question: Why do RFC 8952's authors want captive portals to stop forging DNS and HTTP responses?
options: Because portals need IPv6
It is slow
Because it makes the legitimate network indistinguishable from an attacker, breaks DNSSEC and non-browser apps, and trains users to accept interception
Because HTTP is deprecated
explain: The architecture's first requirement is that solutions must not require forging responses, and should let clients detect TLS interception without human exceptions. Interception by design teaches the wrong habit.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: App permissions and the principle of least privilege
question: Why does an app need to check a runtime permission each time before using it, even if the user granted it last week?
options: It does not; one check is enough
Permissions expire every day
Users can revoke permissions in settings at any time, so a past grant does not guarantee current access
The check unlocks the Secure Enclave
explain: Android's documentation: don't assume permissions have been previously granted; check them before each access. Revocation is a user's control, and apps must handle it gracefully.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Zero-click attacks: from Trident to the Pixel 9 chain
question: A journalist's iPhone gets an Apple threat notification. Which first response best matches the guidance in this lesson's sources?
options: Install an antivirus app from the App Store
Ignore it; zero-click attacks leave no traces
Update the OS, seek expert forensic help (MVT-based analysis by Amnesty's Security Lab or a similar helpline), consider Lockdown Mode, and do not rely on a public-indicator scan alone
Factory reset immediately and discard all backups
explain: Apple says its notifications are high-confidence alerts to take very seriously. MVT's maintainers warn public indicators alone cannot show a device is clean and point to expert help. Wiping first would destroy the evidence analysts need.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: The Chase-Lev deque: two counters and one CAS
question: Why can the owner's take skip the CAS when t < b after lowering bottom?
options: Because thieves only read, they never write top
Because the owner holds a lock on the bottom half
Because a thief can only claim position top, by CAS, and with t < b position b is not top, so no thief can be reaching for slot b
Because x86 makes all loads atomic
explain: Thieves only take position top and must win a CAS to move it. With t < b at least two positions remain, so a thief racing now gets position t, never b. The fence guarantees the owner's reservation of b and a thief's view of bottom are ordered.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Warmup, stable, decay: the schedule and its loss curve
question: You run WSD and save a checkpoint every 5k steps. At 60k steps you decide to train to 100k. Which checkpoint should you continue from?
options: The latest stable-stage checkpoint (60k), continuing at the same constant peak LR
The end of the 6k-step cooldown branch, rewarming the LR to peak
A fresh run from scratch with cosine and T = 100k
explain: The stable stage is the reusable trunk. Continuing it at the same LR needs no rewarm and later gets its own cooldown. (A variant that resumes from the decayed model, WSD-S, where the final S stands for simplified, appears in lesson 6, but plain WSD rolls back to the pre-decay checkpoint.)

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
question: You must produce models at 4 data sizes for each of 5 model sizes. Which plan uses WSD correctly to minimize compute?
options: 20 runs from scratch, each with WSD and a 10% cooldown
1 run of the largest model, with cooldowns used to simulate the smaller models
5 cosine runs with T equal to the longest length, evaluated at 4 intermediate checkpoints
5 long constant LR runs (one per size), each with 4 cooldown branches from checkpoints
explain: Cooldowns replace the data axis, not the model axis: each model size still needs its own trunk. The cosine-checkpoint option is the classic mistake, since mid-run cosine checkpoints are not annealed and underestimate those lengths.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references
question: A proxy splices 1 MiB from one socket to another through a pipe with the default capacity. Each splice moves a full pipe's worth. How many splice calls does it make?
explain: Default capacity is 16 pages, 65,536 bytes. 1,048,576 / 65,536 = 16 rounds, and each round is one splice into the pipe and one out of it: 32 calls. Two would need a 1 MiB pipe (settable with F_SETPIPE_SZ); 256 is the number of 4 KiB pages.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Embedding similarity with label descriptions
question: You rewrite all four label descriptions to be more specific. Which work must be redone?
options: Re-embed every input text and retrain the embedding model
Nothing; cosine similarity is unaffected by wording
Re-embed only the input texts
Re-embed the 4 label descriptions and re-tune the thresholds on labeled data
explain: Input embeddings do not depend on the labels, so they stay valid. The 4 label vectors must be recomputed, and because the cosine scale shifts with wording (bare names topped out at 0.31, descriptions at 0.52 in our example), any threshold has to be chosen again.
